html:
A law passed in 1913 by the parliament of the Union of South Africa that set aside only about 7 percent of the country's land for Black Africans, who were the large majority of the people. It banned them from buying or renting land outside these reserves.

The law also outlawed sharecropping, under which Black farmers worked white-owned land for a share of the crop. Thousands of families were evicted and wandered the roads with their cattle. The writer Sol Plaatje described their suffering in Native Life in South Africa (1916). The newly founded South African Native National Congress, later the African National Congress, sent a delegation to London in protest, without success.

The reserves were enlarged to about 13 percent by a law of 1936. They became the basis of the bantustans, or homelands, of apartheid. The act was repealed in 1991. After 1994, the land restitution programme took 1913 as its cut-off date.
